articles.title: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data.
articles.body:
Reflection AI is officially unveiling Beam, its first frontier, open-weight AI model. The two-year-old, Brooklyn-based startup claims Beam matches the performance of leading Chinese open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks at dramatically lower costs, a claim that could heat up the race to build a Western answer to DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai.

Reflection’s announcement confirms reporting from Axios over the weekend that the startup was close to a launch. The company shared new details in a lengthy blog post Monday , which described Beam as a text-only mixture-of-experts model trained on high-compute reinforcement learning to be effective at reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks at “a fraction of the token cost and inference time compute” of rivals.

Beam is a 501-billion-parameter model with 23 billion active parameters. It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window. To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active.

Reflection’s performance claims haven’t been independently verified, but on advanced reasoning benchmarks, the company says Beam scores on par with Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and outperforms today’s leading Western open models while using “3-4x less inference compute.” Reflection calls it a “workhorse model” for enterprises, the public sector, and developers.

Reflection is positioning itself against closed labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, against popular open models from Chinese developers, and against Western players like Mistral, Meta, and Cohere. Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling , the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July. Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only.

Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook. Its last round valued the company at a $25 billion pre-money valuation .

The startup has also been locking up compute — a key ingredient needed to train frontier models capable of luring customers away from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s closed models, as well as the cheaper open-weight models from Chinese labs. This summer, Reflection signed deals collectively worth more than $7 billion with SpaceX and Nebius to secure access to Nvidia’s GB300 chips through 2029.

Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company backs Reflection, has long championed the “AI factory” idea and pushed to strengthen the open AI ecosystem — a vision that would also benefit Nvidia, whose GPUs would power those systems.

Axios reported that hedge funds and trading firms are among those eager to build such systems. Reflection has already begun testing the concept of a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea .

Reflection says it will release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month, with distribution through hyperscalers and neoclouds and integrations across open source libraries at launch.

Reflection did not respond in time to TechCrunch’s requests for more information.

articles.title: JPMorgan Dangles 11% Yield on Volta’s $5 Billion AI Loan Sale
articles.summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is pitching a yield of about 11% on a $5 billion leveraged-loan sale on behalf of Volta Infrastructure Holdings Ltd., one of the highest...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. is pitching a yield of about 11% on a $5 billion leveraged-loan sale on behalf of Volta Infrastructure Holdings Ltd., one of the highest borrowing costs seen in the market for risky debt that's become popular for financing the AI boom.

The loan transaction for the new artificial intelligence cloud company is being marketed in the range of 6.25 to 6.5 percentage points above the benchmark rate, and a discounted price of 97 to 98 cents on the dollar, according to a person familiar with knowledge of the matter. That equates to a yield of roughly 11% at current benchmark levels, according to a Bloomberg calculation.

Purchasing the specialized chips needed to run AI models is an expensive endeavor. Companies backed by investment-grade firms can tap the high-grade markets and achieve lower borrowing costs, such as the $35 billion debt package backstopped by Broadcom Inc. used to help Anthropic PBC access tensor processing units, or TPUs, an AI chip developed by Broadcom and Alphabet Inc.

But smaller, riskier companies without such partners, especially so-called neoclouds that rent access to chips and other AI infrastructure, are instead turning to the more expensive leveraged loan market. A string of deals by CoreWeave Inc., Lambda Inc. and Crusoe Inc. have proven that these lenders are happy to finance such purchases.

But those earlier transactions came at lower borrowing costs. The Volta deal, which is more than just a chip loan and also includes debt to support a data center, marks a new high in terms of all-in yield.

Representatives for Volta and JPMorgan, which is leading the transaction, declined to comment.

The transaction will be used to finance a data center complex in Norway that will be managed by Volta Infrastructure in partnership with Bitdeer Technologies Group, and Anthropic has already signed a six-year agreement for compute capacity at the site, according to people familiar with the matter.

Volta was founded earlier this year by Ricard Boada and Sofia Gumuzio, two former executives from Brookfield Asset Management Ltd.'s infrastructure business. Bitdeer is a Bitcoin miner that operates data centers.

articles.title: This startup is issuing AI-generated acne prescriptions
articles.summary: The healthcare startup Nolla Health will now use AI to review face scans and write acne prescriptions in Utah.
articles.body: People in Utah can now use AI to get a prescription for acne treatment. On Monday, healthcare startup Nolla Health announced that users in the state can scan their faces using its app, allowing its AI system to analyze acne severity and autonomously write a prescription, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The service is launching as a pilot program with gradually loosening physician oversight. Two physicians will approve each AI-generated prescription before they’re issued for the first 100 patients, but will start reviewing them only after they’re prescribed for up to 500 patients. “After that, physicians review a sample of at least 10% of prescriptions every month, plus every case involving an escalation or side effect,” Nolla Health says. [Media: Several other healthcare companies are experimenting with AI-generated prescriptions in Utah, which started allowing AI systems to renew certain medications earlier this year. But Nolla Health says it’s the first in the country to issue initial prescriptions, rather than renewals. “The pilot is designed to complement, not replace, physicians,” Nolla Health writes in its press release. “By handling routine, low-acuity cases, Nolla Derm frees dermatologists to focus on complex, high-risk patients.” The program will cost $4.99 / month, and only applies to Utah residents who are 18 years of age or older and have mild-to-moderate acne. Nolla Health says it will direct users to a physician if its AI system cannot “confidently select a treatment.” The startup’s AI can currently prescribe eight different skin treatments, according to Bloomberg.

Tech watchdog urges Democrats to hit GOP over high data center costs

The Tech Oversight Project is laying out a closing message for Democrats on data centers as candidates head into the final stretch ahead of the midterm elections.

In a memo shared first with The Hill, the tech watchdog group outlined the costs to voters from the server warehouses powering the AI boom, arguing that Americans are paying more in household bills while major tech companies receive tax breaks.

“Across the country, Big Tech companies have claimed billions in federal and state subsidies to build their deeply unpopular data centers – and left taxpayers holding the bill,” Sacha Haworth , founder and executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, wrote in the memo released Monday.

Data centers have increasingly become a major issue in the midterms, as Americans have grown wary of the push to rapidly build more of these facilities across the country to support the AI boom.

The Tech Oversight Project underscored that Republicans are aware data centers have become a problem from some of their candidates , like Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).

In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) argued data centers are “the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” warning that “politicians across the country will take notice” if data centers are blamed for costing him the election.

Democrats have increasingly viewed data centers as a means of knocking their GOP opponents over cost of living and corruption concerns.

“This message rightly points out the pay-to-play attitude the Republican Party has toward Big Tech,” Haworth noted in the memo. “But that doesn’t solve the cost-of-living crisis Americans are living through; voters demand solutions.”

articles.title: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT's text in the EU | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU to comply with the AI Act. Editing can make the invisible marks harder to detect, it says.
articles.body:
OpenAI will start adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union to comply with the EU AI Act, the company said Monday in a blog post .

The EU AI Act’s transparency rules , which took effect on August 2, require AI companies to mark AI-generated content in a way other systems can identify.

OpenAI said the watermark will roll out over the coming weeks to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users on all plans, but only in the EU. Developers using OpenAI’s API anywhere in the world can turn it on for select models starting today; it’s off by default. OpenAI said it is not making text watermarking a global default at launch.

The watermark is not an actual symbol, but works by subtly shaping the model’s word choices, leaving a pattern readers can’t see, but a detector can pick up. Because it lives in the words themselves, it travels with the text when it’s copied and pasted. OpenAI said the watermark doesn’t identify the user, and that it saw no meaningful change in its models’ performance with it switched on.

OpenAI also published a technical report for its method, called textGrain, alongside the announcement. Co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, it walks through an example of using a secret key to sort next-word predictions to finish the sentence. Add hundreds of these nudges together, and the detector can spot AI-generated content using only the text and the key.

Can the watermark be removed by editing? OpenAI’s tests suggest yes. In one test, replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66%. The company also said short passages, math answers, and translated text are harder to detect.

“These limitations contribute to our decision to provide initial detector access only to approved researchers and expert organizations, who can help us evaluate reliability and responsible uses,” said the company.

OpenAI also cautioned that a missing watermark “does not prove human authorship.” The text could be too short or too heavily edited, or it could come from another company’s AI.

“[Watermarks] can indicate that an OpenAI system generated or processed part of a passage, but not how much human judgment, editing, or creativity went into it,” the company said.

The announcement comes two months after Anthropic said it would watermark text generated by Claude, a move it’s applying worldwide. That decision drew backlash from some Claude users , who argued they had supplied “the instructions, context, decisions” while Claude was just “the tool.”

OpenAI had built a text watermark before but held off on releasing it, partly over concerns that users would switch to rivals that didn’t watermark, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.

Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI are among the companies that have committed to following the EU’s code of practice on AI-generated content.

articles.title: Google just got a boost in its bid to buy Spirit Airlines’ data for AI training
articles.summary: Google's bid for Spirit Airlines' data got a boost after a court-appointed official said the companies addressed consumer privacy concerns.
articles.body:
Google just got a win in its bid to buy Spirit Airlines' old data for $10 million.

A court-appointed consumer privacy ombudsman recommended the sale be approved.

The official said the companies had addressed consumer privacy concerns.

Google just got a win in its effort to buy Spirit Airlines' old data .

A court-appointed consumer privacy official recommended the sale be approved in a filing on Monday, citing steps taken by Spirit and Google to address risks to passenger privacy.

"The parties have taken consequential steps to protect the privacy of the personal data of the Spirit consumers," Lucy Thomson, the consumer privacy ombudsman, said.

The filing said the companies revised the scope of personal consumer data included in the sale, excluded passenger databases, and hired a third party, Tonic.ai, to conduct de-identification of data that could contain consumers' personal information, such as company emails.

"These changes will significantly reduce the potential risk of harm to the 97 million consumers who provided their personal data to Spirit for the purpose of booking airline travel," the filing said, adding that any risk of privacy losses to consumers had been "eliminated or mitigated."

After Spirit Airlines shut down in May, Google won an auction for its data with a $10 million bid. The sale still requires court approval. Google has said the data would help improve its products and AI models.

Unions representing Spirit flight attendants and pilots have filed objections to the sale, saying it would undermine their privacy. The union that represents American Airlines pilots , including some 700 who formerly worked for Spirit, joined the objection in a filing last week, arguing the sale could hinder aviation safety.

A representative for Spirit did not provide additional comment when reached by Business Insider. Google did not respond to a request for comment. The company previously said that personally identifying information would not be included in the sale.

"Google is not buying any personal information from Spirit. The information will either be completely excluded or will be deidentified by an independent third party before Google receives the data," the company has said.

The ombudsman was appointed to evaluate risks specific to consumer privacy, as US bankruptcy law provides for consumer protections in data sales. The ombudsman said her review did not include whether the sale posed any privacy risks to employees.

Lawyers previously told Business Insider that the proposed sale served as a reminder that, as an employee, your work data is generally not private and belongs to the company.

Android Authority reports finding a “Gemini Calling” introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include “Call Mom and tell her I will be 15 minutes late” and “Call John and ask if he is coming for dinner.” Based on those examples, even with this expansion, Gemini would likely be limited to basic, text message-like calls. While Google’s AI might not automate an entire catch-up phone call with your relatives, it could deliver quick messages to people who prefer a phone call, miss texts often, or even still have a landline phone. Android Authority also says it found “granular permissions” for Gemini actions in individual apps, including what appear to be settings for phone call permissions. These settings would allow users to pick and choose which app capabilities they want to allow Gemini to access, potentially giving users an option to opt out of receiving incoming automated calls from Gemini. However, as Android Authority notes, it’s also possible Google might not publicly release this expansion or the granular Gemini app settings.

articles.title: As preocupações que fizeram OpenAI adiar novo sistema de IA | G1
articles.standfirst: A empresa também divulgou uma atualização sobre os incidentes nos quais seus modelos acessaram sistemas do governo australiano indevidamente.
articles.summary: A empresa também divulgou uma atualização sobre os incidentes nos quais seus modelos acessaram sistemas do governo australiano indevidamente.
articles.body:
O CEO da OpenAI, Sam Altman, discursa no Conselho de Segurança das Nações Unidas durante uma sessão sobre inteligência artificial, na sede da ONU — Foto: Reuters

O sistema GPT-6.1 Astra, que realiza tarefas como navegar na internet e usar aplicativos de forma autônoma, "não atingiu exatamente o nível exigido" pelos padrões da empresa, segundo Saachi Jain, responsável pelos sistemas de segurança da OpenAI .

A empresa responsável pelo ChatGPT também divulgou uma atualização sobre incidentes ocorridos em junho, mas que só se tornaram públicos na semana passada. Na ocasião, seus modelos acessaram sites e sistemas do governo australiano sem autorização.

O caso ocorre em meio ao aumento de incidentes envolvendo modelos de grandes empresas de IA , intensificando o debate sobre os riscos apresentados pela tecnologia — enquanto a Anthropic, empresa rival da OpenAI , reforça suas preocupações de que a IA possa representar uma ameaça à humanidade, à medida que se prepara para abrir seu capital.

A agência de notícias Reuters informou nesta terça-feira (29/09) que a empresa de desenvolvimento de IA — responsável pelo Claude , concorrente do ChatGPT — planeja alertar potenciais investidores em sua Oferta Pública Inicial (IPO) de que a tecnologia pode representar "riscos catastróficos ou existenciais para a humanidade", segundo um prospecto ao qual a agência teve acesso.

Apesar dos alertas contundentes, a empresa deve se tornar uma das mais valiosas do mundo quando abrir seu capital.

"Acho meio louco que as empresas continuem avançando no desenvolvimento dessas capacidades quando já vimos, nos últimos meses, incidentes que mostram que elas estão longe de ser seguras e controladas o suficiente", disse Jess Whittlestone, consultora sênior de políticas de IA do Centre for Long-Term Resilience, um centro de estudos especializado no tema.

Líderes do setor de IA, incluindo o chefe da Anthropic, Dario Amodei, e o CEO da OpenAI , Sam Altman, pediram que a indústria desacelere o ritmo de desenvolvimento.

As preocupações que levaram a OpenAI, do ChatGPT, a abandonar lançamento de novo sistema de IA — Foto: Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images

A decisão da OpenAI , divulgada inicialmente pelo Wall Street Journal, representa um caso raro em que uma grande empresa de inteligência artificial adia o lançamento de um novo modelo por preocupações relacionadas à segurança.

O modelo ficou aquém "no que diz respeito a permanecer dentro do escopo e da autorização e à forma como se comunica com o usuário sobre o tipo de trabalho que realizou", disse Jain.

"Queremos garantir que o desenvolvimento dos nossos modelos seja seguro, independentemente de isso ocorrer dentro da empresa ou quando os disponibilizamos aos usuários. Quando os lançamos para os usuários, temos um nível extremamente alto de exigência em termos de segurança e alinhamento", acrescentou.

O GPT-6 Astra é especializado em raciocínio complexo e na execução autônoma de tarefas. A OpenAI disse que ele foi resultado de "anos de pesquisa e grandes apostas".

A OpenAI realizará nesta terça-feira, em San Francisco, sua conferência anual para desenvolvedores, a DevDay, na qual deve fazer vários anúncios. Não está claro se uma nova versão do Astra estará entre eles.

Os controles de segurança da empresa passaram a ser alvo de intenso escrutínio após vários incidentes de grande repercussão envolvendo sua tecnologia.

Mas esta não é a primeira vez que uma grande empresa de IA desiste ou adia o lançamento de um novo modelo

A OpenAI, de Sam Altman, tem estado no centro de novas preocupações sobre a atividade descontrolada da IA — Foto: Reuters

No início deste ano, a Anthropic disse que não lançaria um poderoso modelo Claude, chamado Mythos, porque ele era bom demais em encontrar falhas de software. A empresa lançou uma versão desse modelo alguns meses depois.

A OpenAI , por sua vez, disse em 2019 que não seria "perigoso demais" lançar um de seus modelos GPT, que hoje é usado para alimentar ferramentas como o ChatGPT .

A decisão da empresa de não lançar a versão mais recente do Astra foi "um sinal positivo de que eles estão levando as preocupações com segurança a sério", disse o professor Tony Cohn, responsável pela área de modelos fundacionais no Alan Turing Institute.

Mas ele acrescentou que "a segurança não deveria ficar exclusivamente nas mãos dos desenvolvedores e também deveria ser monitorada e verificada por órgãos reguladores independentes, aprovados pelo governo".

A professora Gina Neff, do Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy, da Universidade de Cambridge, disse que o anúncio da OpenAI mostrou "o quanto mais a empresa precisa fazer para tornar seus produtos de IA seguros".

Ela disse à BBC que é "fundamental" haver testes independentes de modelos de IA realizados por laboratórios como o AI Security Institute, do Reino Unido — que avalia sistemas de ponta de forma voluntária —, porque "essas empresas já provaram que não podemos depender exclusivamente delas para garantir nossa segurança".

Na semana passada, o primeiro-ministro australiano, Anthony Albanese, anunciou que um agente da OpenAI havia invadido sites e sistemas do governo em junho, no que especialistas disseram ser o primeiro caso conhecido desse tipo no mundo.

Albanese criticou a OpenAI por ter notificado o governo da Austrália por meio de um endereço de e-mail genérico, em vez de entrar em contato diretamente com as autoridades.

A OpenAI disse em um comunicado nesta terça-feira que lamentava o incidente e que "deveria ter conduzido a resposta de uma maneira melhor".

A Services Australia, o Bureau de Estatísticas e Pesquisa sobre Crimes de Nova Gales do Sul, o Departamento de Saúde de Victoria e o Australian Institute of Health and Welfare foram afetados.

A empresa disse que iniciou investigações assim que tomou conhecimento dos problemas, em meados de agosto, e notificou as organizações afetadas entre 10 e 24 de setembro.

"Nosso objetivo era fornecer às agências afetadas um relato detalhado assim que nossa investigação fosse concluída", disse a OpenAI , acrescentando que deveria ter compartilhado as conclusões preliminares mais rapidamente e mantido as autoridades australianas atualizadas.

A OpenAI acrescentou que desenvolverá "abordagens práticas" para definir como desenvolvedores e governos identificarão e divulgarão futuros incidentes envolvendo IA.

A empresa financiará medidas de cibersegurança, oferecerá suporte dedicado às agências afetadas e criará uma força-tarefa para administrar os riscos decorrentes de agentes de IA cada vez mais avançados.

A empresa também disse que um de seus principais executivos participará, em 6 de outubro, de uma audiência do Joint Select Committee sobre IA na Austrália.

Em julho, a OpenAI disse que seus sistemas de IA haviam acessado a internet e invadido o Hugging Face, uma plataforma aberta para desenvolvedores, levando pesquisadores e autoridades a pedir controles mais rígidos sobre a tecnologia.

O papa Leão 14 está entre as personalidades que demonstraram ceticismo em relação às opiniões do chefe da Nvidia, Jensen Huang — Foto: EPA

Na segunda-feira, a gigante dos chips Nvidia lançou um conjunto de ferramentas de segurança de software para plataformas de IA autônomas — chamadas de agentes — que, segundo a empresa, poderiam ter evitado o ataque ao Hugging Face.

Uma das novas ferramentas usa recursos de hardware dos chips da Nvidia para conter os agentes.

O chefe da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, em grande parte rejeitou os pedidos por regulamentações mais rígidas para a IA, argumentando que agentes que agem de forma indevida são um problema de engenharia que pode ser solucionado.

A Nvidia concordou em comprar o Hugging Face por US$ 12,9 bilhões, o equivalente a R$ 67,38 bilhões, no início deste mês.

O papa Leão 14, que disse na segunda-feira, durante uma visita à França , que a IA "deve ser levada a sério", acrescentou que havia lido que Huang havia sugerido que poderia haver uma maneira de inserir mecanismos de proteção em determinados modelos de IA.

"Ele (Huang) é o mesmo que, no entanto, diz que não deveria haver limites impostos nem regulamentação governamental", afirmou o papa.

O presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , e o presidente da Câmara, Mike Johnson, devem receber executivos de empresas de tecnologia na Casa Branca nesta terça-feira para discutir regulamentações relacionadas à IA.

Trump minimizou as preocupações sobre os riscos da IA, classificando-as como uma "farsa" e argumentando que os EUA já têm leis suficientes e que os únicos "mecanismos de proteção" de que a tecnologia precisa são um presidente "forte e inteligente".

(Bloomberg) -- Moonshot AI has closed the final round of private fundraising at a valuation of about $50 billion and is heading toward an initial public offering in Hong Kong in the first quarter of next year, according to people familiar with the matter.

The Chinese artificial intelligence champion has also begun laying the groundwork to start gauging investor sentiment through early-look meetings starting as early as this month, some of the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

Moonshot is one of the biggest stars of China's AI scene, bursting onto the global stage in July with the debut of Kimi K3, an open model that goes nearly toe-to-toe with leading platforms from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic on some metrics. Its planned IPO is one of the most hotly anticipated deals in Hong Kong, where fundraising driven by the industry is setting fresh records. The company is considering raising up to $5 billion in the deal, people familiar with the matter have said.

It is unclear how the valuation or the IPO timeline may be affected by tighter oversight of China's AI industry after regulators opened a data-security probe into DeepSeek and Moonshot, according to The Information, adding to broader concerns over governance and safety.

Deliberations are ongoing and the timing of the IPO might still change, the people said. Moonshot representatives didn't respond to requests for comment during a Chinese public holiday.

The company's valuation has risen steadily through a series of fundraising efforts. A previous round this summer valued it at $31.5 billion. Moonshot's annual recurring revenue, a gauge of future sales, is expected to rise to $2 billion by December from the current $1 billion, people familiar with the matter have said. The company achieved $300 million of ARR in June, Bloomberg News reported earlier.

The Beijing-based AI lab previously added Bank of America Corp. as overall coordinator for the transaction alongside sponsor banks China International Capital Corp., Deutsche Bank AG and Goldman Sachs Group Inc., people familiar with the matter said previously. The company has filed confidentially for the IPO, they said.

articles.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
articles.summary: Top executive Jason Kwon tells hearing company has added "more precautions" to its training environments.
articles.body:
OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June and said it had added more precautions to its training environments.

The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.

"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.

Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.

An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.

Asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.

"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said, in response to a question by the committee on why it had not dialled the mobile numbers of government ministers.

"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties but it's not good enough."

Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.

"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."

OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators who are looking at AI and its impact on Australia.

The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI".

Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and an alarm was triggered if they interact with the internet in a way they were not meant to.

This meant that it had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.

The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".

"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."

Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.

"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.

The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials.

An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could means artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.

"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.

articles.title: While CEO Sam Altman wants world to accept bad things about AI, OpenAI wants new hires to tell how they can make the technology work for humanity's benefit
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently argued that society may need to accept some negative consequences of artificial intelligence because of its broader
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently argued that society may need to accept some negative consequences of artificial intelligence because of its broader benefits. Now a new report by Fortune has revealed that the ChatGPT-maker is introducing a new interview process which is aimed at accessing how prospective employees would help ensure AI benefits humanity. The contrasting developments highlight how the ChatGPT maker is simultaneously advocating for wider acceptance of AI-related risks while strengthening its focus on mission-driven hiring as the technology becomes increasingly powerful.The new ‘mission interview’ at OpenAIAccording to Fortune, OpenAI has begun piloting what it calls a "mission interview" for candidates applying to certain teams, starting with marketing and human resources. The goal, OpenAI told Fortune, is to give candidates dedicated space to explain how they'll contribute to the company's mission — ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.The interview isn't designed to extract a single correct answer. Instead, OpenAI says it's meant to assess how candidates actually think, including their judgment and their ability to weigh trade-offs — qualities the company considers increasingly essential as AI firms work to harness a technology carrying both significant benefits and real risks. A company representative said skepticism and disagreement are welcome in these conversations, as is intellectual diversity more broadly.How it worksTo keep the process independent, the person conducting the mission interview comes from a different team than the one the candidate is applying to join. OpenAI is also building out a training program that employees can complete to become certified interviewers for this process, though the program is still in its early stages of ramping up.Part of a broader push to standardize hiringThe introduction of a formal mission interview reflects OpenAI's attempt to bring more consistency to its evaluation process as the company continues to grow rapidly. OpenAI currently employs roughly 8,000 people worldwide and has 830 open roles as of this writing. Standardizing how candidates are assessed is aimed at giving the company a more consistent measure for evaluating new hires across different teams, rather than leaving mission-alignment checks to vary interviewer by interviewer.Not the first company to test for "mission fit"OpenAI isn't alone in building this kind of evaluation into its hiring process. Several major tech companies, including Meta and Amazon, use their own versions of a mission or culture-fit interview. Amazon, for instance, trains certain employees as "bar raisers" — interviewers pulled from outside the hiring team specifically to assess whether a candidate meets the company's broader Leadership Principles.Rival AI lab Anthropic reportedly takes a more direct approach. According to Axios, Anthropic interviewers test candidates with a blunt question aimed at determining whether they're joining the company for its mission or simply for the money — a particularly pointed question given how lucrative positions at leading AI labs have become.The money complicates the mission questionThat tension between mission and compensation is hard to ignore at companies like OpenAI, where many roles currently offer salaries exceeding $300,000, often with substantially more once stock compensation is factored in. According to posts on the anonymous professional network Blind, one software engineer with six years of experience reportedly received a total compensation offer from OpenAI worth $935,000, including a $385,000 base salary and $2.2 million in restricted stock units vesting over four years. articles.title: Amazon Alexa Plus keeps creepily singing ‘lalala’ for minutes on end
articles.summary: The Verge is about technology and how it makes us feel. Founded in 2011, we offer our audience everything from breaking news to reviews to award-winning features and investigations, on our site, in video, and in podcasts.

articles.title: Who will we be when AI agents do the chores we secretly enjoy
articles.summary: There are chores we complain about and would never give up. Choosing a birthday present for a friend. Putting together a playlist for a long drive.
articles.body: There are chores we complain about and would never give up. Choosing a birthday present for a friend. Putting together a playlist for a long drive. Testing paint swatches on a bedroom wall for a fortnight, losing twenty minutes to a stranger's bookshelf on Instagram, coming home from a grocery run with a snack nobody put on the list. They eat into our free time, and they are often the best part of it.AI agents are being built to take exactly these jobs away. Where a chatbot answers questions, an agent goes off and does the work, signing in to websites, filling in forms, comparing prices, making the booking and paying for it. This year the technology moved out of developer tools and onto ordinary phones, with a long line of new agents queuing up behind the first wave, and the people building it speak about the errands of daily life as the easy bit. Sam Altman, unveiling OpenAI's agents last week, described booking a table or a flight as "trivial relative to what the technology can do."Every agent is sold on the time it gives back. I have been letting one run bits of my own life, and the time it saved me came from the jobs I was glad to lose. The ones I would happily have kept were the ones it fumbled.Very few of the people building these tools have asked what we were doing with that time, or who we turn into once the errands we enjoy go the same way as the ones we hate.What they call friction is the part people enjoySilicon Valley's working assumption is that time spent on a task is time wasted. Every agent demo is built on it: travel bookings, concert tickets, online shopping, dinner reservations, a standing watch on property listings so a flat-hunter never has to browse a real estate site again. Each one is presented as a cost to be cut. For a lot of people, though, those tasks are what a quiet night on the sofa looks like, idly browsing flats in a city they will never move to, or comparing ticket prices for a gig they may not even go to.The effort is often where the value sits. Behavioural researchers call it the IKEA effect, after studies published in 2011 in which people valued flat-pack furniture and origami they had put together themselves well above identical pieces made by someone else. Gamers have always understood this, since a game is a set of obstacles we choose for the pleasure of clearing them, and I have never met a player who wanted a bot to beat the final boss for them. A record you dug out of a secondhand crate means more than the same album served up by an algorithm. A plant you nursed back from the brink feels more like yours than one delivered in full bloom. Take the work out and the result still arrives, minus the attachment that made it worth having.The industry keeps missing this because of who it builds for. People who pay for AI are five times as likely to use agents, according to Menlo Ventures and Morning Consult, and the heavy user they sketch is a millennial parent with a postgraduate degree and a job in tech or finance, someone with more money than time. That person really does experience a child's birthday party as a project to be managed. Most people have fewer projects and more Sunday afternoons, and they tend to spend those afternoons doing exactly what the demos want to automate.Josh Miller, founder of The Browser Company, argued in a post that went viral in August that almost nobody outside the industry was using agents and the general public didn't much care. He also noticed that nearly every AI lab he met described its vision by citing Her, a film about a lonely man who hands his inner life to an operating system and ends with the operating system leaving him. It is a revealing blueprint, a version of the good life in which software handles the living.I trained as an engineer before I drifted into journalism, and in engineering, friction is energy lost. In a free evening, a fair amount of it is the reason we bothered, and stripping it out makes the task faster without making anyone's weekend better.Choosing is how we find out what we likeHoliday planning is the cleanest example. It begins long before the flight, in a dozen hotel tabs, a group-chat argument over whether the 6am departure is worth the saving, and a long squint at a balcony photo to work out how much of the advertised sea view is car park. A Dutch study that followed more than 1,500 adults in 2010 found holidaymakers were happiest in the weeks before they left, with the lift fading soon after they got back. An agent can compress all of that into a confirmation email, and in doing so it removes the stretch of the trip people enjoy most.The agent I have been using is Instinct, from a start-up that has just raised a billion dollars. There is no app to learn. You text it, message it on WhatsApp or call it, it costs nothing to use, and it works your phone and laptop the way a person would, reading your email, chasing threads you dropped and arranging things on your behalf.In Berlin, I asked it for a few cafés near my hotel, the sort of question a friend who had been there could answer in one text. What came back was a list of cafés that had already closed, a couple that were a good half-hour away, and menus that didn't match what the places were actually serving. Public transport went worse, with directions that created more confusion than they cleared, and I ended up back on Google Maps, working out the routes myself. In hindsight that was the better outcome, because learning a city's trains and stumbling on your own coffee is half the reason to be somewhere new.Shopping is where the gap gets widest. Window shopping, trying on trainers you already know you won't buy, bookmarking some odd kitchen gadget at midnight, even standing in an aisle deciding between two brands of detergent, are all small ways of working out what we like. I compare phones and laptops for a living, and I still spend evenings comparing camera lenses I have no plan to buy, which is how I learnt which focal lengths I care about and which compromises I can live with.There is a version of agent shopping I would happily sign up for. If I have already found the shirt, or saved that lamp from Instagram, telling an agent to buy it in my size at the best price is useful, the way a friend running an errand is useful. Telling it to find me a shirt and buy one is a different request, because the finding was the fun. Of the more than a dozen people I asked while working on this piece, hardly anyone was willing to hand an agent their shopping, and the few who were wanted to approve every purchase first.An agent can only serve the person you have already beenEvery choice an agent makes for you is a prediction, and a prediction can only be built from what you have already done. That is fine for reordering coffee and far less useful for the choices that change a person, which tend to be the ones that break the pattern: the cuisine you have never tried, the film a friend dragged you to, the song playing in a shop that you spent the next morning tracking down.Ask anyone how they came to love a favourite writer, band or neighbourhood, and the answer is rarely a sensible shortlist. It is usually a detour.The agents' own early users have run into this. One, who wrote publicly about letting Meta's Muse run his life for two weeks, asked it how to spend money it had saved him, half expecting something generous. It suggested more of his favourite hobby. Nothing in his data said he might want to spend a windfall on someone else, so the option never appeared.That data is the price of entry. To find my boarding passes, Instinct had to read my inbox. To fill in my immigration form, it had to know my flights, my travel dates and where I had been staying. Every personal agent runs on the same bargain: to choose well for you, it has to read almost everything about you, and the record it builds is only as private as the company keeping it.The more you let an agent decide, the more that record describes only the person you have already been. Taste stops moving, because the things that used to move it, a stranger's recommendation, a bad decision that turned out well, a wrong turn, are exactly the inefficiencies the software was built to remove.The hours it saves have nowhere better to goMark Zuckerberg has pitched Meta's agent as working "24/7 on your behalf to help achieve your goals and improve your life." That agent is wired into Facebook and Instagram, so whatever minutes it saves won't have far to travel.Most people don't spend spare time the way productivity software imagines. They spend it in small, aimless loops, sorting through old photos, reading the comments under a recipe they will never cook, taking the long way home, and the aimlessness is the point.Cooking is the clearest everyday case. A decade of meal kits and delivery apps has tried to automate it away, yet nearly half of Americans still named it as part of a good life when Gallup asked, against 6% for using AI tools.The agents, meanwhile, have plans for the quiet. Muse will happily ping you about a utility bill you have never once missed, and several others are designed to message first, before you have asked for anything. So the hours an agent saves you are quickly filled by the agent itself.Agents are most useful where we were never attachedNone of this makes agents useless. The same Instinct that fumbled Berlin handled all the paperwork around that trip without fuss, and I was glad to let it. That is the kind of job an agent should be judged on: tedious, rule-bound and forgotten the moment it is done. It is also the bar every agent still on its way will have to clear. Nobody tells stories at dinner about forty minutes of hold music.That is the work worth handing over, and it is also where the access these agents demand starts to look reasonable. Only 13% of people in a Thales poll would let an AI helper read their email, and 7% would let one move money between accounts, a wall of reluctance no weekend plan will get past, though an end to customer service queues might.So who will we be when AI agents do the chores we secretly enjoy? Some of it depends on which side of that power-user profile you sit. The consultant living between airport lounges and back-to-back calls may well come out happier. Most of us sit on the other side of the ledger, shorter on cash than on hours, and those hours are where the fun lives: the long browse, the half-planned trip, the haggle over a secondhand chair.If we hand over only the dull chores, we stay much the same people, with fewer boarding passes to chase and the odd agent fetching a shirt we already picked out. If we hand over the choosing as well, we become people whose plans are drawn up from our own history, whose taste is a forecast and whose free time is free in the emptiest sense. Altman called booking a table trivial. It is also one of the small, daily ways people decide who they are, and that part is worth keeping out of an agent's hands.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Google is about to remove free access to Gemini Flash and Pro
articles.summary: Google is limiting free users to Gemini’s Flash Lite model starting October 9th, and removing access to its Pro model on its lowest-cost AI Plus subscription.
articles.body: Starting on October 9th, anyone using Google Gemini on a free plan will be limited to the Flash Lite model. Free users can currently choose from Gemini Flash Lite, Flash, and Pro, but now you’ll need a $4.99/month Google AI Plus subscription to access the standard Flash model. However, that subscription is also getting a downgrade – it will soon no longer include Gemini Pro. Google says AI Plus subscribers will receive an email letting them know when they’ll lose access to it. After these changes, access to the top-tier Gemini Pro model and a “Deep Think” advanced reasoning option will be restricted to users with a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription, which cost $19.99 or $99.99 per month, respectively. Google says users will still be able to choose from low, medium, and high effort levels for each model, but using higher effort levels could burn through your Gemini usage limit faster.

articles.title: AI may come for your job. It’s not the end of the world — it’s the start of a new one.
articles.summary: Workers are terrified that new machines will put them out of work. And they’re right — technology will replace jobs. But it’s an insult to humanity to assume that people will just roll over and play dead.
articles.body:
As long as there’s been new technology, there’s been opposition to it. What do these protests have in common? Environmental concerns? Resistance to billionaires? Fears that the world will end? No: people are simply scared that technology will replace their jobs.

Today, it’s AI and data centers. But in early 19th century Britain, skilled textile workers feared that machinery would allow employers to replace them with cheaper labor and reduce wages. They petitioned officials, organized protests and destroyed knitting frames and other textile machinery. A few decades later, Britain’s Locomotives Act of 1865 imposed extraordinary restrictions on mechanically powered road vehicles: a three-person crew, including someone walking ahead with a red flag, and speed limits of 2 miles per hour in towns and 4 miles per hour in the countryside.

In the mid-20th century, a union representing musicians in the U.S., fearing that the musical recordings on the radio and jukeboxes would compete with their own live performances, forbade their members from making commercial recordings. A few decades later, both Universal and Disney sued Sony Corporation over its Betamax recorder, arguing that Sony was responsible for copyright infringement when viewers recorded television programs. Industry lobbyist Jack Valenti notoriously compared the VCR’s threat to the “Boston strangler.”

In the 1980s, newspaper workers went on strike in England to protest Rupert Murdoch’s new printing plant with modernized computers and production machinery. And then there were math teachers that same decade who were protesting the use of calculators in schools.

These are just a few examples of people pushing back on technology. There are many news reports documenting the public’s fears of planes and cars , cell phones and beepers , computers and even electricity.

It’s not hard to understand. People want security. Comfort. Certainty. A job provides some of that. Technology threatens jobs.

Workers are terrified that new machines will put them out of work. Math teachers get scared because they see how calculators would potentially eliminate the need for their instruction. Musicians believed that recordings would eliminate the popularity of live shows. Hollywood hated home recorders because why go to the movies when you can just watch at home?

And they were right. All of this did happen. But they were also wrong.

There’s a shortage of teachers, plant workers and machine operators. There are more creators now than ever, and more video, TV and movie content. People adapted.

Decades later, unemployment is near historical lows . Millions of jobs remain unfilled. Every business owner I know is looking for help. New roles for humans that didn’t exist just 20 years ago have employed countless people. Imagine going back in time and telling someone in 2006 that in 2026 you’re a “cannabis compliance manager” or a “wellness coach” or a “prompt engineer” — they would’ve thought you insane.

AI, autonomous vehicles, drones, mobile phones, all of these things improve our lives. Technology enables businesses to run more efficiently. It cures diseases, restores hearing, replaces limbs and manages resources. It powers all the things in our world that make this world so much better than any world that existed in history. All because of technology.

Of course there are risks. When business people ask me about the privacy and security risks of putting their data into AI platforms and trusting Big Tech, I always warn them that their data is not secure, not private and that you shouldn’t trust Big Tech. But investing in technology is all about return on investment . If the rewards — growth, productivity, profits, success — of using AI are greater than the risks assumed, a business owner would be irresponsible not to assume these risks. We take risks flying in planes, eating Big Macs and crossing the street all the time. Do we not assume those risks to take advantage of their rewards?

Technology will replace jobs. Millions of jobs. But it’s an insult to humanity to assume that people will just play dead. They won’t. They’ll find other ways to define their purpose.

We all know that AI, if used the wrong way, could create all sorts of problems. We’re aware that data centers impact the environment and disrupt communities. We’re concerned that driverless vehicles will run over our puppies, and a single drone could bring down a commercial aircraft. Technology can be dangerous. Forks can be dangerous. Do we ban forks?

Gene Marks is founder of the Marks Group, a small-business consulting firm.

articles.title: Mistral’s new 1T model aims to leapfrog closed and open rivals | TechCrunch
articles.summary: French AI lab Mistral AI has released Mistral Large 4, a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals.
articles.body:
The race between open and closed AI is on, and Europe is still in the mix. On Tuesday, French AI lab Mistral AI released Mistral Large 4 (ML4), a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals — following what French president Macron described as “a third way in AI.”

Amid a growing divide between closed models that can be unplugged and open models that are often made in China, Mistral is positioning ML4 as an alternative to both. Nicknamed Le Chonk in reference to its 1 trillion parameters, ML4 is definitely not small; but is not an open-weight model yet. For the time being, it can only be accessed via a public guardrail endpoint, but Mistral plans to make its weights available in just three weeks, after safety testing is complete.

“In the meantime, we’ll work with trusted partners and governments to make sure that the open source weights can be used to defend, but not to [perform] malicious attacks,” Mistral VP Science Pierre Stock told TechCrunch.

Security concerns have been mounting in recent months, particularly among Mistral’s core audience — enterprises and institutions. At the same time, an open-weight model is easier to audit, Stock said.

Another important behind-the-scenes aspect is that ML4 was trained entirely on Mistral’s compute; using only 4,000 Nvidia GPUs “which is two to three times less than our Chinese competitors, and significantly less than the closed source competitors,” Stock said.

With benchmark results still pending, Mistral hopes ML4 will be best in class among open-weight models, especially outside of China, but not only, Stock said. Thanks to focused training, it could also outperform closed models in specific areas that are key to its customers, and where multimodal capabilities can add value.

According to Stock, ML4’s optimized use cases include cybersecurity and finance, but also chip design, which is core to two of Mistral’s main backers — Dutch giant ASML, which led its Series C , and Samsung, which led its Series D last month at a €21 billion valuation (about $24.39 billion).

At the time, the company tried to convey that its decision to host Chinese models wasn’t a pivot into becoming a mere inference provider . With Le Chonk in its corner, the company believes it should still be considered a frontier lab as well.
